title: Pasta Primavera
subtitle: spring pasta with green vegetables
excerpt: A bright, light pasta made with the best of the spring vegetable patch. Asparagus, peas, courgette and spinach are barely cooked and tossed with pasta and a little Parmesan. This is fast, fresh cooking at its simplest.
sourceNotes: Pasta primavera, meaning spring pasta, is an Italian-American invention popularised in New York in the 1970s. It has since been widely adopted in Italy as a seasonal celebration of spring vegetables.

content.text: Add the vegetables to the pan in order of how long they need. Asparagus takes longer than spinach. Do not overcook -- these should all stay bright green and have a little bite.

items.prepNote: woody ends snapped off, cut into 4cm pieces

content.text: Cook the pasta in well-salted boiling water until al dente. Reserve a large mug of pasta water. Drain and set aside.
Heat the olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute. Add the asparagus and courgette. Fry for 4 minutes until just tender and lightly coloured.
Add the peas and cook for 2 minutes. Add the spinach and stir until it wilts, about 1 minute.
Add the drained pasta to the pan. Add a good splash of pasta water. Toss everything together over medium heat for 1 to 2 minutes.
Remove from the heat. Add the lemon zest and a squeeze of lemon juice. Add half the Parmesan and toss again.
Serve in warm bowls with the remaining Parmesan and a crack of black pepper.

items.fix: Keep cooking times short. Serve immediately after tossing. Asparagus and peas should still be vibrant green.
Add more reserved pasta water and toss again. The starchy water creates a light sauce.

content.text: Pasta primavera is a spring celebration. Use whatever looks best at the market. Broad beans, green beans and peas all work. The formula is simple: green vegetables, olive oil, lemon, Parmesan.
